speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If the first Bill is passed, the Second and Third Readings of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 2) Bill will follow.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I do not stand on this podium very often, and for good reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The mandate and powers provided to the military are clear and focused, and necessarily scoped by Parliament to keep within this remit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In peace, that legislation is usually adequate for the Armed Forces' crucial task of national defence, to organise themselves to build capabilities and protect the sovereignty and security of her country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For militaries that are often at war, or operating in periods of tension, legislative changes are more frequent, as varied conditions require timely adaptations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But during peace, one does not expect frequent changes to legal provisions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are thankful that Singapore has enjoyed a period of prolonged peace since our Independence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be other amendments which I will go through with Members, and they are related to discipline and administrative processes to update and to ensure the smooth functioning of SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF, incepted 57 years ago in 1965, has been a military constantly on the move.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of you would have witnessed it through the years growing up; NSmen lived through it and some here are actually responsible for pieces of that transformation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From 13-tonne AMX-13 light tanks to 70-tonne Leopard main battle tanks; wooden hull ships to stealth frigates; Hawker Hunters to F16s, F15s and, in a few years, F35s, the SAF today is a modernised military, capable of prosecuting missions across the spectrum of security threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singaporeans, too, have seen this SAF journey every year, through the National Day Parades (NDPs) when we allow SAF to play on the Floating Platform, Padang or National Stadium and into the heartlands.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That display will take place in a few days' time on 9 August.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I hope that Members will enjoy the dynamic display.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We, in this House, and Singaporeans out there are not the only ones who have noticed this impressive and progressive march.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Asian Military Review described the SAF as "one of the most well-trained and equipped forces in Asia Pacific".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That others notice the SAF's competency and growing ability is good, and the core of deterrence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For SAF commanders and troops, DIS affects primarily the intelligence community, and we call it the C4I community – Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, let me shift focus there to explain what needs to be done and why, by the DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To protect Singapore, the Army, Navy and Air Force have built up capabilities in their respective domains on land, at sea and air.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is not enough for each service to do so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Command and control are essential to maximise effects by orchestrating joint efforts, so that the whole is greater than the sum of the parts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Pari passu, intelligence capabilities had to grow in tandem, to keep pace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The C4I community has been growing alongside the three kinetic services, less visible but no less progressive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: C4I operations have grown over the years, too, for example, in counter-terrorism, from our operations, from our NDPs to key high-security multilateral events, like the Trump-Kim Summit and ASEAN Summit in 2018.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: C4I soldiers were deployed for counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency operations in Kuwait and Afghanistan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our imagery analyst teams were part of the Combined Joint Task Force Headquarters in Kuwait from 2014 to 2016.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Then-US Secretary of Defense Ashton Carter expressed his appreciation for their contributions which helped stop ISIS' terror campaign.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even despite these impressive developments and achievements hitherto, the C4I community's role has been largely that of a supporting agency, akin to combat support, logistics and maintenance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They enable the Army, Navy and Air Force to achieve their missions by providing actionable timely intelligence and ensuring that communications are secure to execute plans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And these responsibilities will still be part of DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, what then has changed to require DIS to be a fully-fledged military service arm?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And over the years, I have updated Members in this House about these security threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2015, I spoke about "hybrid warfare", "an orchestrated campaign" which "integrates the use of conventional and unconventional tools of warfare" to "fracture the solidarity of the target nation".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I quoted former Chief of General Staff of the Russian Federation, General Valery Gerasimov, who said, "The very rules of war have changed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The role of non-military means of achieving political and strategic goals has grown and, in many cases, they have exceeded the power of force of weapons in their effectiveness." Reflect on this statement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are all familiar with the dictum "political power grows out of the barrel of the gun".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And he says, "In many cases, the non-military means of achieving political and strategic goals have exceeded the power of the force of weapons".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I described this concept as the exact antagonist of our Total Defence concept.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To respond to the growing prevalence of hybrid warfare back then, I pointed out that SAF will have to contend with cyber threats and the growing use of disinformation in warfare.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2016, I shared about the unidentified hackers attacking Ukraine's power grid and disrupting electricity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2017, the Financial Times wrote on cyber warfare.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Looking back over those years, this generation is witnessing real-time, and personally, the changing face of warfare.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even as the public experiences it first-hand, this realisation by militaries of vulnerabilities and opportunities within the digital domain has not been uniform.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some militaries adapted earlier than others to the "Gerasimov Doctrine" and have steadily been building capabilities on many fronts, including the digital domain, for example, the German military that incorporated a new service, as we are proposing today, in 2017, to defend the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Baltic States I visited recently have also beefed up their capabilities in their military and civilian organisations against digital threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Apart from states, non-state actors have also recognised that they can use the digital domain to achieve their ends, particularly terror cells.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whether to recruit vulnerable inductees, spread false propaganda, supply funds, procure weapons, sabotage or bypass state security systems, these areas have become standard fare for terrorist networks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From a security perspective, we should ask, "what will be the scale of these digital threats going forward and can they threaten the well-being of citizens and even the entire country?" The questions are, of course, rhetorical and I think every Member here knows and agrees that these threats can only grow and have a very real physical impact on any country that is unprepared.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are all convinced because we have seen for ourselves the many forms of cyber intrusions that develop quickly, even within the past few years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Last year, we saw the Colonial Pipeline cyber attack that cut off gas supplies to many South and East Coast states in the United States and disrupted the lives of countless people.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Earlier this year in February, a cyber attack on the European telco, Vodafone, restricted cellular communications for millions of people in Portugal.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be horrendous, but not unthinkable, about the potential fallout from attacks on water systems, hospitals, air traffic, trains, financial systems, pension systems – the list goes on.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, cyber threats, disparate in form and source, occur in the thousands, even millions, each day.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, they should be differentiated from the ones that have the most pernicious intent and seek to undermine our nation's sovereignty or security.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the SAF, it has asked itself this simple question, just as it does if the threat came from air, land or sea: how does it detect, mitigate or repel any potential aggressor, an orchestrated cyber attack by state and non-state actors that mean to do Singapore and Singaporeans harm?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the digital domain, the fourth service is the force on the frontline, as it should be.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are thankful that hitherto, our intelligence agencies have not detected any campaign against Singapore of that nature in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we should not wait for one and it would be prudent to start and build up the fourth service now.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As with the mission of the three existing services, DIS will ensure Singapore is defended against the full spectrum of threats against potential aggressors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The digital environment is more porous than the physical one, but DIS will be responsible to guard against these aggressors in that domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the SAF, DIS will protect its networks and systems and strengthen our soldiers' commitment and resilience in operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will also continue to provide accurate, relevant and timely intelligence to support SAF operations and capitalise on cutting-edge digital technologies to advance SAF's digitalisation as a networked force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For threats to Singapore's internal environment – and this, I am referring to the digital environment, similar to the SAF's support to the whole-of-Government for counter-terrorism – DIS will work closely with the Home Team, CSA and other national agencies to leverage one another's strengths in protecting Singapore's digital networks and providing a strong digital defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This also requires related changes to other Acts to ensure that the legal statutes can be properly applied to DIS soldiers as well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Therefore, section 2(1) of the Interpretation Act 1965 and section 27(5) of the Wills Act 1838 are amended to respectively include DIS in the definition of "military" when used in relation to Singapore's military, and to include in the definition of "soldier", a reference to a DIS serviceman.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 21(2) of the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act 1906 is amended to include DIS within the scope of that provision.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Like the Service Chiefs of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the CDI will be a member of the Armed Forces Council and have legal powers to discharge his or her duties and authority to lead DIS in times of conflict.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sections 2(1), 8(1), and 8B(2) are amended to effect these changes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Based on the SAF Act and Constitution, the Chief of Defence Force and Service Chiefs are appointed by the President acting in her discretion.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 111 is amended to allow the three-year limitation period for the trial of offences in military courts to commence later in certain situations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF Act 1972 currently requires a serviceman to be tried within three years from the date of commission of the offence, or the date of reporting of the offence to a disciplinary officer or a military policeman, whichever is later, after which he can no longer be dealt with under the SAF Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is referred to as the default limitation period.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, in some cases where both military and civilian offences have been committed by the same offender, time is required for Police investigations or related civil court proceedings to conclude, so as to allow MINDEF to assess all available and relevant information, before deciding whether to charge a serviceman for a related military offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, where Police investigations have commenced for a related civil offence before the end of the default limitation period, therefore, the three-year limitation period will commence from the date those investigations end.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, if court proceedings for a related civil offence are instituted in a civil court before the end of the default limitation period, the three-year limitation period will commence from the date that those proceedings end.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the person is sentenced to imprisonment, detention or reformative training, the limitation period will commence from the date on which the person completes the sentence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the person is sentenced to imprisonment, detention or reformative training before the end of the default limitation period for any unrelated civil offence, the three-year limitation period will commence from the date on which the person completes the sentence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fourth, if an arrest warrant was issued before the end of the default limitation period and could not be executed within that period despite all reasonable efforts as the whereabouts of the accused were unknown, the three-year limitation period will commence only on the date the person is arrested.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Any charges in the military court would be for discrete and separate military offences to be dealt with in the military courts after the conclusion of the civil court proceedings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These new time limits for military court trials will also apply to summary trials, in accordance with section 78(3), as the considerations are similar.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Currently, all military offences under the SAF Act have to be dealt with either by summary trial or the military courts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is no option for MINDEF to offer composition for minor military offences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Designated officers will be authorised by the Armed Forces Council to offer composition to such offenders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To effect these changes, a new section 79A will be created to provide for the composition of military offences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sections 60 and 62(1) will also be amended to define an "authorised composition officer", and to provide for the disciplinary option to refer an accused serviceman to an authorised composition officer to compound the offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The new section 79A will provide that the authorised composition officer is not to be in the same chain of command as the accused serviceman.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will ensure that an independent officer assesses the circumstances of the case before making an offer of composition.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Presently, service offences committed under the Civil Defence Act 1986 are dealt by a disciplinary officer or the civilian courts, while disciplinary offences committed under the Police Force Act 2004 are dealt by disciplinary proceedings or the civilian courts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similar to the SAF, there is no option for SCDF or SPF, respectively, to offer composition for minor service or disciplinary offences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Designated officers will be authorised by Commissioner SCDF or Commissioner of Police, respectively, to offer composition to offenders who meet the criteria.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To effect these changes in the Civil Defence Act 1986, a new section 85A will be inserted to provide for the composition of service offences committed by full-time National Servicemen, NSmen, volunteer ex-NSmen and auxiliary members.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 70(1) will be amended to provide for the above-mentioned officers to be referred to an authorised composition officer for composition of the offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Similarly, in the Police Force Act 2004, a new section 84A will be inserted to provide for the composition of disciplinary offences committed by special police officers, which refer to full-time National Servicemen, NSmen, volunteer ex-NSmen and volunteers serving under the Special Constabulary.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It also provides for special police officers to be referred to an authorised composition officer for composition of the offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Just like in the SAF Act, the amendments to the Civil Defence Act 1986 and Police Force Act 2004 will provide that the authorised composition officer is not to be in the same chain of command as the accused serviceman and will ensure that an independent officer assesses the circumstances of the case before making an offer of composition.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is an accepted principle for financial penalties to keep pace with inflation and increases in wages and allowances for adequate deterrence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The fine limits imposable by the Subordinate Military Court under section 118(7) will be increased.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The fine limit for a Senior Disciplinary Committee under section 72(6)(b)(ii) will similarly be increased from $10,000 to $30,000.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These increases also take reference from civilian courts and are similar to the District Courts' fine limit, which is currently set at $30,000 in the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The maximum fines imposable by Disciplinary Officers in the SAF who deal with minor offences by Summary Trial will also be increased correspondingly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the lowest tier, a Junior Disciplinary Officer will be able to impose on a soldier of third sergeant rank and below a maximum fine of $600, up from $300.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The most senior Disciplinary Officer is the Chief of Defence Force, who will be able to impose a maximum fine of $10,000, up from $6,000.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These proposed fine limits do not exceed the Magistrates' Courts' fine limit, which is currently set at $10,000.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sections 68, 69, 70, 70A, 70B, 72(6) and 118(7) are amended to effect the above changes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF Act currently provides for a maximum five-year imprisonment sentence for any insubordinate behaviour, including the act of assaulting a superior officer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In contrast, the Penal Code provides for a maximum imprisonment sentence of seven years for someone who abets an SAF serviceman in assaulting his superior.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Therefore, an inconsistency exists, as the abettor can be punished more harshly than the actual offender.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The proposal, therefore, increases the maximum imprisonment sentence for the act of assaulting a superior officer from five to seven years if the act was committed during active service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These changes remove the disparity with the punishment for abetment in the Penal Code.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be no changes to the penalties for other acts of insubordination.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The amendment in section 112(1) is to maintain consistency of punishment powers of the military and civil courts for the same civil offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Maximum punishments that may be imposed by a military court for a civil offence tried under section 112 are aligned with those which may be awarded by a civil court subsequent to changes in the relevant legislation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For civil offences for which caning can be imposed by a civil court, the military court would be able to impose caning for those same offences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The proposed amendments to section 72(1) on power of a Senior Disciplinary Committee will provide that a senior military expert of or above the rank of ME8, when created, will be subject to the same disciplinary processes as an officer of or above the rank of Brigadier-General.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Next, proposed amendments are made to the administrative processes within the SAF Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 129 is amended to allow the Military Court of Appeal to serve court appeal documents via other means, including sending to an electronic mail address designated by the appellant in the notice of appeal.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is already the practice in civil courts; we are just catching up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 167 is amended to clarify that suspected deserters arrested by SPF may be released instead of being brought before a civil court.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Currently, an SAF serviceman arrested by the Police for Absence Without Official Leave or Desertion shall be taken as soon as possible before a civil court.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is no option for the Police to take any other course of action.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The present amendment now gives the Police the option to release such arrested persons instead of bringing them before the civil court.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This, thus, aligns the SAF Act with Article 9(4) of the Constitution which requires that an arrested person be either released or brought before a Magistrate within 48 hours.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Amendments are proposed to section 205A to provide that the regulations made under section 205A(1) may provide for the Armed Forces Council to determine rates and contributions of various superannuation benefits by issuing General Orders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These superannuation benefits refer to the SAVER Plan or Premium Plan for our uniformed Officers, Warrant Officers and Specialists.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Section 205C is amended to remove the requirement for a periodic examination of the SAVER-Premium Fund.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF Act currently requires an actuarial examination of the SAVER-Premium Fund to be conducted at least once in five years because the fund had a "Defined Benefit" portion.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, with the removal of this portion in 2006, there is no longer such a need.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore and Singaporeans have enjoyed peace and progress these past six decades since our Independence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From an improbable nation, we have defied the odds time and again, to maintain our sovereignty and way of life to become one of the leading cities in Asia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These three services have formed the core of Singapore's armed forces ever since.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reality of digital threats has been recognised for some time and have been raised in the course of MINDEF's Committee of Supply (COS) debates for several years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Earlier this year, Minister Ng Eng Hen addressed this issue during this year's COS and foreshadowed the creation of the Digital and Intelligence Services (DIS) Unit in the course of this year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The digital domain is undoubtedly critical in our daily life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our bank records, health records, transactions with Government and even daily expenditure are all increasingly electronic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why each institution that deals with electronic data needs to ensure the security of that data and the integrity of those systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Important infrastructure and daily operations are also dependent on technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Earlier in his speech, Minister Ng highlighted how fuel shortages across the US East Coast in May last year were due to ransomware attacks on the Colonial Pipeline.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another example raised during the COS debates was how Iranians could not top up their gas and petrol stations in October last year because the payment systems were hacked.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a matter of international law, it is unlawful for a state to target civilian infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I would argue that this should cover digital attacks on civilian infrastructure to disable their operations as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is much debate on this however, and not all experts are agreed that such attacks would constitute violations of international law and the prohibitions against armed conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, there is also difficulty of pinpointing whether an attack originated from a specific state, especially if it takes place in the digital domain and many of these attacks may continue to persist even in times of peace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It does not take much imagination to expect that military technology and infrastructure, which is increasingly dependent on technology, can also be subject to digital attacks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As we move to more automated warfare, including the use of unmanned aerial vehicles, we must also equally protect the technology that drives those new systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To me, there is no doubt that the digital domain is as important as the kinetic one and countries are just as vulnerable to serious disruption and paralysis from digital attacks as they would be from kinetic ones.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Based on the Minister's speech introducing this Bill, I understand that the creation of this new DIS is an evolution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The DIS will be evolving from the existing C4I unit: Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have a few clarifications for the Minister for Defence on this topic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, when does the Minister expect the DIS to be operationally ready?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, currently the C4I team supports the operations of the Army, Navy and Air Force and is an integral part to their operations planning.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would the DIS continue to deploy people into the other services to support their operations?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, given the significantly different skills involved in the DIS as compared to the rest of the armed forces, would DIS recruits and employees be required to go through the same type of training as other parts of the armed forces are, such as, for example, BMT and IPPT?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If so, is there a chance we may lose people who have special talents in the cyber domain, but who may not have other military skills?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would the DIS also be staffed with civilians, for example, rather than uniformed military personnel?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And would the chief of the DIS be a civilian?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fifth, would the DIS also take over responsibility for intelligence gathering for the whole armed forces, or would each of the services, such as the Army, Navy and Air Force, still have their own intelligence capabilities?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The final point on the first Bill is this – and this is actually a question that is interesting from an internal law perspective as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would Singapore consider an attack on our key civilian or military digital infrastructure by a foreign state actor a hostile act in contravention of international law?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has important implications, for example, on whether and how we believe we would be entitled to respond in the event we are subject to such attacks, including, for example, whether hackers are legitimate targets in the event of such an attack.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do have a short comment for the Constitution (Amendment) Bill and since it is a short Bill, the comment is short.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note that the commander of the DIS is going to be put on the same level as the other service chiefs, such as those in the Army, Navy and Air Force, and it will be one of the appointees in which the President has a discretion to approve.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is similar to the power the President has in relation to other key public appointments including Permanent Secretaries and the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, of course, makes the Chief of the DIS more difficult to appoint and replace in the event there is a disagreement between the Government and the President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But given the importance of this appointment, I think it is necessary to have this safeguard.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, if the chief is going to be a military person, then, this is not an issue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is timely, given the growing importance of cyber warfare and cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Cyber warfare involves attacks on critical infrastructure systems of an adversary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These could include "soft kills" that damage key operating software or hardware without kinetic action, such as through hacking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The objective is to weaken the target country by compromising its core systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Cyber attackers may conduct espionage using spear-phishing attacks to gain remote access to an adversary's computer to extract sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They may hack critical infrastructure like the electrical power grid, which will disrupt communications and even cause deaths if, say, life-supporting medical equipment is shut down.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Or they may crash modern economic facilities like banks and payment systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Propaganda attacks may be employed to control the hearts and minds of the people living in the targeted country or make them lose faith in their own country and sympathise with the enemy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They have been employed by nation-states for many years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the digitalisation of almost everything, the cyber threat is increasing by the day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Up until recently, a war was usually fought by sending the air force to bomb the target nation's critical infrastructure and defence installations before any ground troops were sent in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In modern warfare, cyber attacks are likely to be one of the first modes of attack, because they can be employed so easily without any detection – the Gerasimov doctrine, which the Minister alluded to earlier in his speech.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The DIS aims to bolster SAF's capability to defend Singapore in the digital battlefield.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the establishment of the DIS, the other armed services must be careful not to develop a mindset that the DIS alone is responsible for all things digital in SAF.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the commercial world, there is now much less distinction between tech companies and non-tech companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Fourth Industrial Revolution has forced all companies to become technology companies in some form or shape.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those that do not digitalise will find themselves losing customers to more digital-savvy competitors and may even go out of business.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, in the military realm, every armed service – the Army, Navy, Air Force and DIS – will need to use digital capabilities to keep ahead of our nation's potential adversaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Digitalisation, cyber defence and cybersecurity cannot be left to the DIS alone to handle.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister share the broad parameters regarding which digital responsibilities fall under the purview of DIS and which do not?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The DIS will not be the first technology-focused agency to be set up within the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope DIS, CSA, HTX and GovTech plan to establish a common communication platform, so as to not only share information occasionally but actively work together on a regular basis to counter the cyber threats that Singapore faces.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that a Digital Ops-Tech Centre will be established as a centre of excellence for SAF's digital expertise, partnering with the Defence Tech Community, whole-of-Government digital agencies, academia and the industry, to remain innovative in its approaches and culture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister elaborate more on how this partnership will work in practice?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The DIS will likely have significant capabilities and powers to intrude in the private space of the functionaries of would-be adversaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What protections are in place to make sure that such capabilities are not turned on citizens or abused?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is necessary in any developed democracy to put in place legal safeguards and channels for recourse to prevent the abuse of power by current and future governments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One form of oversight would be for MINDEF to provide confidential reports to a cross-party Parliamentary Select Committee for Defence, which can then scrutinise those reports and ask questions in a confidential setting.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that DIS will focus efforts to attract and develop both military and non-uniformed digital experts to grow SAF's digital workforce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will DIS be engaging technology contractors to supplement their own manpower?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, how will it ensure that the contractors and their employees, who may be reporting to foreign managers based in other countries, how will they ensure that they would not leak sensitive information?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Members will recall how Edward Snowden, who leaked highly classified information from the US National Security Agency (NSA), was not an NSA employee but a contractor with a consulting firm hired by the agency.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The need for security clearance will naturally limit the pool of manpower available to DIS, in what is already a very competitive labour market for tech talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will make it a challenge to find sufficient local tech talent to join DIS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the introduction of the DIS could further draw talent away from the private sector, as many Singaporean tech workers are likely to be attracted to the pay, benefits and job stability that DIS has to offer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In order to expand the pool of tech manpower, our Polytechnics and local Universities must urgently increase enrolment in IT and technology-related majors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a point I raised before in this House.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More funding should be provided to our local institutions to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will benefit the recruitment pipeline of both DIS and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to know that NSFs and NSmen with tech talents will be leveraged to support the SAF's digital core.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, zero-day vulnerabilities are software or hardware bugs in systems that have yet to be discovered or patched by the developer or manufacturer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When governments or individuals discover these "zero-days", they can create software code to exploit the vulnerabilities, known as "zero-day exploits".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Zero-day exploits can potentially enable their owner to access sensitive information in other computer systems or take control of those systems remotely, often undetected.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One of the most well-known zero-day exploits is Stuxnet, a cyber operation that sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would assume, but will not ask the Minister to confirm, that the role of DIS will include building capabilities to conduct offensive cyber operations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the course of this, DIS may discover and stockpile zero-day vulnerabilities in operating systems that run critical infrastructure and the military networks of potential adversaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It would be natural for DIS to want to keep the knowledge of these exploits secret, so that our potential adversaries do not patch their systems and DIS maintains its offensive capability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there is an offence-defence trade-off between stockpiling zero-day exploits and helping other local Government agencies and private organisations patch these vulnerabilities so our own critical infrastructure does not get hacked by others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2016, a group of hackers calling themselves the Shadow Brokers released a cache of top-secret cyber spying capabilities that likely belonged to NSA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of these included zero-day exploits, which could be used to exploit vulnerabilities in products produced by companies like CISCO, Juniper and Fortinet, that protect US companies and critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The existence of these zero-days raised questions about whether NSA should have told the vendors about these vulnerabilities, so that the vendors could patch them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The US Government has a policy, whereby, any agency that wishes to keep a zero-day exploit has to argue their case through what is known as a Vulnerability Equities Process (VEP).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The VEP comprises an Equities Review Board chaired by the National Security Council and attended by senior officials from agencies concerned with the security of critical infrastructure, like the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Commerce.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The last point I wish to raise concerns the potential for commercialising defence technologies to benefit Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many technologies that we use every day originated from military technology.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, invented TCP/IP, which is the plumbing that makes the Internet possible.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Global Positioning System, or GPS, was originally developed by the US Department of Defense and is now used in almost all our mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Israel is widely recognised as a "startup nation".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of Israel's high-tech companies were founded by soldiers who completed their National Service in Unit 8200, the Intelligence Corps of the Israel Defense Forces.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, we hardly hear of commercial technology or tech start-ups originating from the Defence Tech Community.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I can understand why MINDEF would rather not share any defence technology discoveries publicly, because that may cause us to lose our edge over our adversaries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the establishment of the DIS, there is likely going to be billions of dollars from the public purse spent on developing digital capabilities within the SAF.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There should be some scope for allowing some limited commercialisation of defence technologies that would benefit our nation, economy and society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The interaction between defence and commercial technologists could also spark ideas, innovations and discoveries within the DIS and the wider Defence Tech Community, and help the SAF improve its technological edge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In summary, I support the creation of the DIS within the SAF but hope the Minister will consider the points I have raised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, the DIS must not operate in a silo.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All armed services need to continually digitalise in order to maintain their edge on the battlefield.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The DIS should work closely with other digital Government agencies to jointly counter the cyber threats that Singapore faces.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, the establishment of the DIS will create a greater demand for local tech talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Local higher education institutions must increase the intake of Singaporeans in IT-related majors to meet this demand.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.05 pm until 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Warfare has moved away from conventional means as technology now pervades all aspects of our lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the Minister for Defence indicated in his opening, sovereignty is now being challenged, even in the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the last decade, threats to society have made their presence felt in the digital sphere – scams, organised crime, misinformation campaigns, cyber disruptions of critical services and transnational hacking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The overall concept of cyber attacks is not new.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These attacks seek to infiltrate and disrupt vital data services and systems, conduct sabotage, espionage or manipulation, resulting in damage to the state and even widespread casualty and loss of life if critical infrastructure is affected.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The consequences of hybrid warfare are no less than those of physical conventional warfare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Sophisticated and large-scale cyber warfare used to be something that we associated with the distant future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But as technology advances rapidly, societies and governments around the world have developed greater reliance on digital infrastructure and data storage capabilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Naturally, this leads to higher stakes in the cyber domain when it comes to national security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, we do not have to search our imagination to envisage the impact of extensive cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The war waged by Russia on Ukraine rages on, involving a hybrid of physical and cyber attacks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Following that, several important Ukrainian nuclear power companies, media firms and government entities were also compromised.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many Singaporeans, the Ukraine crisis is a stark reminder that "we must never lose the ability to defend or look after ourselves" – to quote Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is imperative that we maintain our security and stability through a strong, capable and credible SAF that includes building up our digital intelligence and defence capabilities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This, of course, is not a new journey as we had introduced digital defence as a new sixth pillar of Total Defence in 2019.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But an organisation is only as good as the people it has.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I will focus my speech on the people in DIS, in particular, and in SAF in general.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened that recruitment and talent development efforts are underway for DIS.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As I mentioned, people are at the heart of all organisations and we must spare no effort to nurture them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In turn, they would serve four years of National Service.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I seek a few clarifications in this regard and related matters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can SAF define how these NSFs and NSmen will be selected for DIS?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How does differentiated National Service models impact other arms of SAF?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What is the current size of the initial core of our DIS and what is the plan and rate of ramping up?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are there also plans to expand the scheme to other tertiary institutions that will offer relevant foundational courses beyond NTU?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What efforts will be taken to retain suitable talent after National Service (NS) is up for our NSFs?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can SAF offer remuneration, benefits and a career that can rival some of our most sought-after tech companies?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do we also ensure that our personnel involved would be highly security-conscious, who practise excellent cyber hygiene and do not flout secrecy laws?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have had instances of information leaks even by experienced civil servants at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The damage to our national security would be very serious if this happens in the cybersecurity set up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, candidates must be specially picked and trained so that they do not commit these errors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, because certain NSmen or NSFs will have particular access to sensitive data, will the Ministry consider a moratorium on them becoming employees of foreign governments or organisations when they leave DIS without prior permission from MINDEF?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is also some misplaced concern that new vocations within DIS may be seen or regarded as a more comfortable vocation to serve NS obligations compared to the other services.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a potentially damaging mindset to have as it would adversely affect the morale of our soldiers within the wider SAF.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All NS vocations come with high amounts of responsibilities and stress, and should be respected and regarded seriously as such.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, my view is that DIS offers an opportunity for women in Singapore to contribute towards our efforts for a strong digital core.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The cybersecurity industry faces a talent crunch, and the Government has been investing in efforts to better involve women in the field.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has to be a whole-of-nation effort encompassing the relevant organisations, such as social media platforms, cybersecurity groups and also our citizens.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do seek some clarifications from the Minister regarding some details of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And, if so, what are the security safeguards in place to ensure national security?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have full confidence in our Armed Forces and its personnel.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, clearly spelt out regulations will ensure that all personnel will know the legal limits of their operational work and ensure surveillance investigation and other actions will be taken in full compliance with the law, including if the service is expected to work with other Government agencies, Next, this Bill also introduces the concept of the composition of offences to the disciplinary regimes of SAF, the Civil Defence and the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Why is this considered to be a positive enhancement of the disciplinary regime?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I recall from my experience in SAF some years ago as an NSman, as well as a unit disciplinary officer, that the conviction, pursuant to a summary trial, will be captured in the records of an errant serviceman and may possibly affect the performance assessment of such servicemen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And, if so, will this be a relevant factor, for the purposes of the assessment of the serviceman's performance and his promotion prospects?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, if compounded offences are scrubbed from the personnel records, will the records not show an inaccurate picture of a serviceman's disciplinary records, with misdemeanours and commission of less, so-called "serious offences" not being reflected?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, may I also ask the Minister to elaborate a little on the guidelines for the independent disciplinary officers deciding on whether to allow the serviceman to compound the offence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, will a repeat of a similar offence by a serviceman disallow the independent disciplinary officer to compound the offence again?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I note that this Bill is enhancing the existing maximum punishments under the SAF Act, which can be awarded for certain offences, as well as by the relevant officers assigned to officiate summary trials.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Clauses 12 to 7 increase the current fine amounts that may be awarded in a summary trial by a disciplinary officer or a senior disciplinary committee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Besides the reasons given by the hon Minister in his speech for the enhancement of the punishment under the SAF Act, may I also ask the Minister whether there has been a significant or proportionate increase in summary trials and our convictions at summary trials in the last five or 10 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And, if so, whether this plays a part in the Government deciding to enhance the punishments?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While military action can occur across any geographic feature and training has to be as realistic as possible, the impact of military equipment could well be damaging and polluting to the waterways and its surroundings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does PUB have complete say in its pre-exercise or pre-training assessment of the environmental impact of the proposed SAF training?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does PUB have a continuing duty to supervise the training being carried out on the ground, so that PUB is able to ensure that the actual environmental impact of any SAF training in any of its public reservoirs or waterways is minimised?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If not, can PUB be given such a power to supervise the actual use of its lands and waterways by the SAF?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The establishment of the Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS) as SAF's fourth standalone arm is timely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But this is also not new to SAF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill will allow SAF to develop and scale up its operational capabilities to respond to modern welfare.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will speak on three key areas: the importance of DIS, ways to expand the manpower catchment pool for DIS and the projected scale and size of the outfit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been weaponised; the use of cyber warfare has increased over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can either scale up and incorporate advanced technologies in our Armed Forces, or increasingly falter behind other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, DIS can, and must, leverage new technological capabilities to make up for our manpower constraints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The number of NSmen is projected to fall in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: DIS can make up for manpower constraints by integrating and expanding our capabilities in the virtual terrain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Talent pool is critical for any tech outfit to succeed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, on grappling with the war on tech talent in Singapore and, in fact, globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Competition for tech talent in Singapore will continue to be heated with firms aggressively raising wages and other benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Other top talents command even higher salaries and that is straight from school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A key difference between working for DIS and private companies is undoubtedly the mission in serving the nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, wages are a hygiene factor that we must address.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Ministry share its plans to effectively attract top talent, considering the intense competition from Big Tech firms and startups?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we also attract Singaporean talent currently working overseas?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Digital natives are clearly the future backbone of DIS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In some countries, many 18 to 21-year-olds are selected to join military and intelligence services even while in school.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Preparatory programmes are offered to them to develop their skills and also pique their interest in serving the nation in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We could explore the possibility of developing such feeder programmes for our youths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe this would suitably complement the top-tier scholarships for digital and intelligence talents for which the Ministry has already planned.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As service in the DIS may not be as physically demanding as compared to the existing tri-services of SAF, joining DIS may be a tenable pathway for mid-career SAF servicemen or Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry to consider structuring a pathway for mid-career conversions?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the plans to help mid-career servicemen and women to similarly be trained and transit to DIS?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many countries are already ahead of us in formalising a cyber warfare force in addition to their tri-services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the SAF's C4I Community has been the backbone of the SAF's digital intelligence services over the past decade, the formal establishment of DIS will enable us to scale up our digital capabilities efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Is it also envisioned for DIS to partner with GovTech and other related Government tech agencies as part of the whole-of-Government digital security infrastructure roadmap?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry also share how DIS will strive to keep its knowledge current and cutting-edge, tapping on partnership with the private sector?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The DIS will ensure that our nation is well-equipped to adapt and conquer the evolving face of modern warfare.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also, perhaps, the most significant stride thus far towards building a truly future-proof Next Gen SAF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next week, as other Members in this House have also recognised, Singapore will be celebrating our 57th birthday.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The sovereignty we enjoy today did not come easy and we must never take the peace we enjoy today for granted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ultimately, the success of SAF's mission to safeguard our nation's sovereignty is dependent on the commitment of our servicemen and servicewomen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have four areas of clarification for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the possible intrusion of DIS' activities on civilian life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: DIS has been given a broad remit to tackle cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because its powers are so extensive, there will be concerns that, in its mission to defend Singapore's national security, DIS may track the lives and activities of average Singaporeans, even when there is no clear and significant security purpose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what checks are in place to ensure that DIS' extensive powers are not misused?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry and DIS draw the line between reasonable counterintelligence and excessive surveillance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second area of clarification is on the composition of offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Compounding an offence is significant because it means that no further criminal proceedings will be brought against an accused upon payment of a composition sum.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have several questions arising from a comparison of this Bill and the CPC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, this Bill does not provide for the compounding of the abetment of, conspiracy to commit and attempt to commit a compoundable offence, even though the CPC does.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the schedule to the SAF Act will clarify if such offences may be compounded?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, this Bill does not state that a composition has the effect of an acquittal, even though the CPC does.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if a composition under the SAF Act will either be a "discharge amounting to an acquittal" or a "discharge not amounting to an acquittal"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If a composition will have the effect of a "discharge not amounting to an acquittal", can the Minister clarify whether a composition for a military offence will be considered an antecedent for: first, future military offences and second, civil offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, section 243(1) of the CPC provides that a person authorised under any Act aside from the Penal Code to compound offences must exercise the power of composition subject to the general or special directions of the Public Prosecutor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the Public Prosecutor will provide directions for how authorised composition officers should exercise their composition powers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will every composition decision be subject to the review and authorisation of the Public Prosecutor?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third clarification is on the increased penalties for offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how it arrived at this significant increase?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Were the fines benchmarked against punishments provided under other pieces of legislation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share whether clear sentencing guidelines will be set by the military court to address the transition from the previous ranges for fines to the updated ranges?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is essential, given that the previous sentencing precedents will no longer provide a useful guide on the likely quantum of fines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final clarification is on the limitation period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Military courts do, of course, benefit from waiting for the conclusion of civil proceedings and sentences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we have to balance this against the experience of the accused, who face the prospect of a military trial hanging over their heads for many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Police investigations and civil proceedings can take years to complete.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sentences of imprisonment, detention or training can take years to complete.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together, the accused may have to wait for years, even decades, before their limitation period starts counting down.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if there are specific cases that have prompted such a significant amendment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, were there cases where the three-year limitation period expired while civil proceedings were still ongoing and it negatively affected the conduct of military proceedings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Relatedly, can the Minister share if the military court will also consider the impact of the preceding civil proceedings and any sentences served by the accused for related civil offences when imposing a sentence for the military offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today's battleground is shaped not only by kinetic weapons of war, but by a potent blend of data, technology and innovation that forms our digital world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this age of increased information warfare and information-enabled warfare, the way these advances are deployed will be pivotal in achieving a competitive advantage over adversaries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In an interview, Major-General Robin Anderton-Brown, a director at UK Strategic Command in the UK Ministry of Defence stated: "The term 'domain' in a military sense reflects the fact we traditionally considered Defence in terms of the environmental domains of maritime, land and air, but now there is the growing importance of space – a domain in its own right – as well as the virtual domain of cyber, which affects not just Defence but the whole of society." Other jurisdictions have had similar services.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the US, its Army Cyber Command integrates and conducts cyberspace operations, electromagnetic warfare, and information operations, to ensure dominance in the cyber domain and information warfare.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The UK established its National Cyber Force (NCF), which is a partnership between defence and intelligence in 2020.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is, hence, a need for MINDEF to take the lead here.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Fake news or misinformation and disinformation have been used as weapons during peacetime to de-stabilise a country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen examples, through online campaigns, where terrorist organisations, such as ISIS, recruits and mobilises their members to carry out attacks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have also seen the presence of foreign influence in the 2016 United States presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In times of war, the battlefield is not just about conventional warfare, but we also need to strengthen defence in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is due to cyber attacks and hackings of key institutions with sensitive information.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides cyber attacks, information operations should also be addressed collectively.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An example is the current Russia-Ukraine conflict, where there has been the deployment of information warfare comprising disinformation campaigns and false-flag videos that aim to deceive the public.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These were harnessed to influence public opinion and manipulate information to undermine Ukrainian sovereignty and break their defensive spirit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, when faced with such scenarios, we need MINDEF and the SAF to spearhead our information defence in both wartime and peacetime.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): I would like to raise three areas of concern.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a tight labour market, SAF needs to attract the best talents for our DIS and groom the expertise.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To cite an example, in 2015, the Pentagon launched the Defense Digital Service office (DDS).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Brett Goldstein, the Director of DDS, described his team of technologists, which come from various public/private-sector backgrounds and which includes engineers, designers and developers, as a "SWAT team of nerds" to show the diverse and deep levels of expertise at hand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in the US DDS, although scope is not similar, the team is recruited on a two-year limited appointment to focus on a specific mission; after which they return to the private sector or the academia.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we have to balance this with how SAF protects the sensitivity of information and screening of recruits.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To illustrate this, Dickson Yeo was a Singaporean academic who was arrested by US authorities for being an illegal agent of Chinese intelligence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yeo's former PhD supervisor in LKY School of Public Policy was Chinese US citizen Huang Jing, who was expelled and identified by MHA as an "agent of influence of a foreign country".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This underscores the importance of screening and protection, especially in the fields of cybersecurity, information and intelligence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Within Singapore, DIS has to work on this collectively with other Governmental agencies.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, in the UK, the National Cyber Force (NCF) is part of the UK Ministry of Defence, the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, the Secret Intelligence Service and the Government Communications Headquarters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, SAF's new DIS cannot operate in silo and has to integrate into the whole-of-nation approach to combating the growing digital and information threats now and in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I propose that our DIS officers should have exposure and experience of operations across all SAF services and perhaps, key DIS officers should also have experience and exposure within the various relevant agencies within MHA or MCI.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Across jurisdictions, it is important to have an updated exchange of ideas and innovation in the industry so that the latest of ideas and best-of-class technology can be deployed within DIS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, I welcome the announcement that SAF's CCR will host bilateral and multilateral exercises, bringing together "militaries, industries, and academia" to facilitate information exchange.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Digital defence cannot be done on our own.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would there be efforts to formulate a joint comprehensive defence framework for the region?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will such bilateral or multilateral digital defence take shape in the light of certain geopolitical tension or relations?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope to hear more plans on this from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot just focus on defence per se, but it is important for us to also build up pre-emptive strike capability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I cite two examples from the UK and the US.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Both the stated missions of the UK NCF and US Army Cyber Command can be read to include not just defence, but strike capabilities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In our history, we have not been immune to such disinformation attacks during peace or war time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the Japanese invasion of Malaya and Singapore in World War II, propaganda leaflets were airdropped onto the population.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These leaflets were frequently dropped towards the end of the war and they were varied, depending on the target audiences, and in different languages.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill sends a message to potential attackers and provocateurs that they cannot break our body nor our spirit without a fight.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is apt that in the month of celebrating our nation's 57th year of independence, we table this Bill to further enhance the protection and defence of our nation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Warfare is no longer limited to land, sea and air.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So far, MINDEF has been running our military cyber defence and intelligence teams in the absence of a specific service branch.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MINDEF already has its Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) Community and the Defence Cyber Organisation, which coordinates cybersecurity across the defence sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such an arrangement is quite similar to those in many other countries, such as the United States, Canada, France, the United Kingdom, Australia, Israel and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In these countries, the defence ministries manage cyber defence and military intelligence departments without creating another distinct service branch.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An exception is Germany, which set up its Cyber and Information Domain Service branch to take command of its cyber, IT, military intelligence, geoinformation and operative communication units.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister share, with the House, the Ministry's considerations in creating a separate service branch?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why is this necessary and what are the specific advantages of doing so?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of my greatest concerns is that our resources, in terms of both manpower and finances, are limited.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: National defence is not a sector which we can easily augment with foreign manpower or talents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With a sharp shortage of talent in the IT sector, not just in Singapore but all over the world, what strategies does MINDEF have to beat the competition, particularly the private sector, and hire the right talent to join this service?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The situation is acute as we can only hire Singaporeans who embrace these three hallowed words – duty, honour and country.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They must see the big picture and understand the importance of defending our way of life, with a strong sense of mission and commitment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will the Ministry ensure that the formation of the fourth service will not compromise the defence capabilities of our three existing services?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to ask the Minister if he could elaborate on whether and how the DIS will build our capability in information warfare, like what an European country had conducted against Ukraine in early 2022?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such information campaigns are conducted on various platforms online, capitalising, especially, on the wide-ranging effect of social media.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The concoctions of mashed-up news and fake news using different channels are spread widely and instantaneously.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They seek to influence national and global opinions, to shape policies and developments of political agendas.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such information operations are becoming increasingly more complex and sophisticated.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will we ensure that the hearts and minds of our Singaporeans will be protected against such malicious and nebulous influences?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need communications talent as well to help build the immune system of our psychological defence and to conduct information warfare, when necessary, against hostile state and non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to seeing how the DIS will share with Singaporeans some of its capabilities at our 58th National Day celebrations next year.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are experiencing an avalanche of innovation, opportunity and progress.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For example, today's smartphones are a million times more powerful than the Apollo 11 guidance systems, and a thousand times faster than the Cray-2 supercomputers in the mid-1980s.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There were two billion people online in 2015.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, over five billion people, or 63% of the world, are connected to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The growing dependency on digital systems over the last 20 years has fundamentally changed how societies function, how communities interact and how individuals respond – everything from how we purchase our groceries, travel and play.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Last year, there were over 12 billion IoT active endpoints that manage many critical services and infrastructure, ranging from manufacturing and healthcare to e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: According to the World Economic Forum, cybersecurity measures in place by businesses, governments and individuals today are increasingly made obsolete by the growing sophistication of cyber capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A case in point would be the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack, which impacted the computerised system managing the pipeline and forced the company to shut down operations to contain the attack.
