speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This pipeline carries gasoline, diesel and jet fuel from Texas to as far as New York and delivers about 45% of all energy consumed on the east coast.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This event triggered an emergency declaration for 17 states, including Washington DC, to keep the fuel lines open.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This attack could have happened in Singapore, especially for our critical infrastructure, such as our oil refineries and port and air services.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How differently will we safeguard our critical infrastructure with DIS?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As digitalisation continues to accelerate and remote working capabilities expand into homes due to the pandemic, companies have increased their digital reach and footprint in homes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Workers today have acquired more digital capabilities to work and operate remotely.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With this, every organisation now has a greater variety of connected devices with little protection against a cyber attack.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When well-coordinated, other threats, such as deepfakes and disinformation for hire, can cause disruption and deepen the mistrust among societies, businesses and governments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For example, deepfakes have been used to clone voices to authorise the transfer of monies to fraudulent accounts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In other scenarios, it can influence outcomes and views.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The digital and intelligence operating domain is vastly different from traditional domains.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The spectrum of the intensity of the conflict, the target sets, which include private and public infrastructure, as well as its potential impact, it is dynamic and difficult to attribute.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The notions of force and violence will also be less apparent in the digital domain.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is a difficult operating landscape and will need a flexible, highly adaptable force that has strong partnerships and networks to be effective.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How will the state of victory and defeat be defined in the digital domain?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Similar to the other three services, how does DIS project deterrence in this domain?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As we look deep within the core of the mission of DIS, future capabilities, such as quantum computing, can cause disruptions and inflexions to the security landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Quantum computing is one of those threats that can break existing encryption keys and pose immense security risks to critical data.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The public key encryption is still uncrackable when using very long key pairs with 2,048- or 4,096-bit keys.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: An advanced quantum computer could crack the code in over a few hours.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, the development of advanced quantum computers today will still require 100,000 times more processing power, with a 100 times improved error rate to be viable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This may be over-the-horizon, but we must continue to invest and be ready to guard against these threats as they emerge.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Looking closer to our current state today, an attacker's pathway takes an average of two days to penetrate the company's internal computer systems.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Check Point research reported that there were 50% more attack attempts per week on corporate networks in 2021 than 2020.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These attempts were predominantly on education and research organisations, followed by Government, military and communications.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This offensive threat landscape is coupled with an employment gap of over three million cybersecurity professionals worldwide.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is a dearth of talent with the requisite technical skills.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, the job industry has a high turnover and retaining talent is increasingly difficult, as there are bountiful opportunities to progress.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is much to reflect on as we think of the city of Troy and the Trojan horse, the 300 Spartans and the betrayal at the battle of Thermopylae, and the story of Dune between the Harkonnens and the Atreides.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Hence, we must change and evolve how we fight and defend ourselves.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Like how the US Air Force was formed from the US Army Air Corps, and the US Space Force from the US Air Force, we need a service that can protect our sovereignty in our digital domain.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a week's time, we will celebrate our National Day and we will also celebrate our 55th year of National Service.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Singapore Armed Forces have always protected us from all threats – land, air and sea – and have always evolved to take on any new threats.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The security threat confronting Singapore today is multifaceted and ever-changing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is increasingly evident when we consider countries and non-state entities capable of launching attacks across both physical and digital spheres.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The current war in Ukraine, for example, has shown that Ukraine had been under cyber attacks since 2014 and these intensified just prior to the war in February this year.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cyber attacks targeting a country is nothing new.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2007, a series of cyber attacks targeted Estonian organisations, including its parliament, ministries, banks and newspapers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The online services of Estonian banks and media outlets were taken down by unprecedented levels of internet traffic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Massive waves of spam were sent by botnets and huge amounts of automated online requests swamped servers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just this year, malwares, such as Pipedream and Incontroller, can target ICS and SCADA systems in industries, and can seize control and take down critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I understand the pressing need to develop our defence capabilities to tackle attacks from the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: DIS will include having a Digital Ops-Tech Centre and Centre of Excellence for Cyber Range.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that attacks can originate from countries and non-state entities from across the globe, how does this align with the role of the Cyber Security Agency (CSA)?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With CSA reporting under a different Ministry, how can we ensure that both agencies complement each other and become our force multipliers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, for threats, such as Pipedream and Incontroller, which can seize control of critical infrastructure in Singapore, how will both agencies collaborate across Ministries to provide the best defensive outcome for Singapore, without hindering the operations of each other?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given our scarce resource of talent in this very specialised field, how can we ensure that we efficiently use the limited pool that we have for the best effective outcome, for the security of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On DIS' capabilities, how can we ensure we are constantly seeking cutting edge capabilities and continuously evolve to tackle the ever-changing threats to safeguard our country?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond cyber defence, our DIS must also have capabilities to strive to protect our assets in the digital space.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will we define the new rules of engagement in this digital sphere?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can, or should, DIS operate independently of the other three arms?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And does DIS have some degree of autonomy to deal with cybersecurity threats from any source, state or non-state, quickly and expeditiously to neutralise the threat, without the knowledge of the other arms of SAF?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Part of deterrence is also showcasing our capability and posturing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we intend to showcase the capability of our fourth service as a deterrent measure?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In March 2022, there were 128,100 job vacancies and the ratio of job vacancies to unemployed people is 2.42, the highest since 1998.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, it is already challenging to find Singaporean digital talents for the private industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Setting up DIS will inevitably place additional demand on an already strained labour market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, how can we man this fourth service with the right Singaporean digital talents?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To meet the needs of our industries, we can develop our local workforce with digital skills and complement them with global talents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must keep in mind that for DIS, as is the case with our other three services, our personnel must be Singaporean, as their work deals with national security and interests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Collectively, in Singapore, we cannot just move the local digital talents from one industry to another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, we have to grow a larger pool of local talents to tap on, especially in context of our national defence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will require a whole-of-Government approach over the next few years as we rapidly build our national cyber defence posture and digital capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To meet the short-term ramp-up phase, beyond attempting to attract individual mid-career talents, can we also consider mass career conversion programmes from other industries or even consider upskilling or retraining some of our NSF or NSmen units and redeploying them to DIS, so that we can gather the critical mass required for DIS to be effective quickly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Alternatively, we can also consider having a scheme where NSmen who have completed their ORNS cycle continue to volunteer and support DIS.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Work-Learn Schemes where Digital Specialists can earn academic credits from Nanyang Technological University (NTU) that contribute to a degree in Data Science and AI, Computer Science or Computer Engineering is a very good idea for our NSFs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we expand that idea to also include opportunities for our higher Nitec graduates to acquire skills and gain academic credits for their future diplomas too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as we solve the short-term ramp-up needs of DIS and our industries, do we need to readjust the long-term supply of digital and tech talents graduating from our institutes of higher learning (IHLs)?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What proportion of the future forecasted demand for these talents will be met by our local IHLs?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, should we be looking into increasing our cohort sizes for the digital and tech courses in IHLs to meet the long-term demand?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we keep an eye on costs, it is also important for us to build the right capability to defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Singapore is now facing various security threats.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These range from terrorism to cyber attacks which all have the potential to cripple our nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The ongoing conflict in Ukraine is a stark reminder to take national security issues very seriously and to safeguard Singapore's security physically, as well as in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Personnel deployed in this fourth service must be loyal and true to Singapore, as their task involves our nation’s security and interests.This must be seen as an opportunity for us to contribute towards our nation’s safety and defence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should also be mindful of the costs of setting up DIS.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should remain prudent with our expenditure, without compromising on the efficiency and effectiveness of national security.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, as the range of threats we face become multifaceted and more complex, it indeed important to consider how we can best develop our defensive capabilities as a nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to consider how best to do this given our present capabilities, resources and manpower challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recent world events have highlighted the urgency in which this has to be done.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the last two decades, cyber warfare has been waged openly between the major powers, and increasingly undertaken by middle powers too.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Iran and North Korea are frequently mentioned in the international media, but they are not the only ones.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The bigger concern is that the increased frequency and sophistication of the attacks are happening.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We are seeing more and more use of zero-day exploits being unleashed on IT systems globally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: By zero-day exploits, it means vulnerabilities that not even the authors of the software are aware of, which means IT users can expect limited protection from.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is useful for us to know how the world get to where it is – a cyberspace dominated by the law of the jungle.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And how did IT, which has revolutionised humanity, get weaponised?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And did how this cutting-edge expertise get proliferated?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sadly, the story is similar to that of nuclear weapon proliferation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For many decades, the US, as the birthplace of IT, started as the dominant and sole superpower of cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: After Stuxnet, countries realise that most civilian infrastructure can get compromised through hacks in industrial automation systems.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some countries and groups started building up sophisticated capabilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As early as December 2009, there were reports of coordinated attacks against IT giants like Google, aimed at not just compromising individual systems, but also went after core IP, such as the source codes and proprietary designs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: All data were wiped out and replaced with photographs of burning American flag.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A much larger wave of proliferation happened around half a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In August 2016, a group called The Shadow Brokers publicly claimed that they have hacked into the vault of NSA and stolen a large arsenal of NSA's zero-day exploits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And in April 2017, The Shadow Brokers then shared some of the most powerful codes to the public.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The world, since then, saw more waves of large-scale and sophisticated cyber attacks using tools that were supposedly leaked.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some of the most sophisticated code is now available to groups and nation states.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And because the Internet respects no boundaries, the rest of the world is at risk.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, Ukraine was the initial nexus of the NotPetya attack in 2014.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The attack started through a software update from an Ukrainian tax filing software company.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It quickly jumped onto Ukraine's ministry of health to Chernobyl's radiation monitors, and then to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some global insurers even chose not to pay off the damages as they claim that this damage, even for companies outside of Ukraine, was due to an act of war.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This changing battlefield affects us, for we have unique vulnerabilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The obvious scenario facing SAF is a formal cyber attack as part of hostile military actions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our next generation's SAF pushes C4I to a whole new level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will fuse battlefield intelligence from all services, from near and far, from all parts of the battlefield, to determine the right course of action and get the right assets to respond.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: C4I is at the heart of this coordination.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If our C4I network or military equipment is fully compromised, then a significant amount of SAF's capability could be shut down, even for a short time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But another kind of serious threats that Singapore must be ever ready for, is for global cyber attacks not aimed at Singapore but, nevertheless, spillover through our borders, given that Singapore is the telecommunications, digital, financial and business hub of the region.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am not just talking about digital banking or enterprise software.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our hardware infrastructure, like the rest of the modern countries, rely on industrial automation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We are embracing IoT with a multitude of sensors to manage our city-state.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, our value proposition to the world can be summed up by three words: trust, connectivity and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And all these three pillars can be undermined by cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Beyond attacks on our economy, our society is also vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is entirely possible that Singapore could come under constant attacks from nations with strong cyber capabilities that seek to destabilise our media, civic institutions, or even our political system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And while we have natural vulnerabilities, we must also be cognisant that we are a net importer of IT capabilities and talent, and this makes it harder for us to keep us safe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is an acute shortage of top-notch AI talent here, which is a concern as IT will increasingly power cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sometime ago, I had dinner with a top AI expert in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: He shared with me how, within a few years, the top companies headhunted away the bulk of the teaching staff of AI at Carnegie Mellon University, which is one of the largest and best IT institutions in the US.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, if even the US is short of top-notch IT talents, it is not surprising that Singapore would be short too.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore also lacks sufficient programmers skilled in assembly language.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Assembly language is used to write codes for software to interface with hardware.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For decades, assembly language work is seen as basic, low-level technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As such, only a handful of locations – India, China, Eastern Europe and Taiwan – have deep pools of such skillsets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But over time, the industry realised that assembly language helps a hacker manipulate systems at the architectural level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is also the most appropriate for building malware like viruses and trojans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, assembly language is the go-to choice if someone want to reverse engineer a piece of software that has already been compiled.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Far from being low-level work, assembly language is now seen as a sophisticated mean to subtly hack the chip, device or the telecoms equipment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is what hackers mean when they say, "hacking down to the metal".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is a skill shortage that is not easy for most countries, including Singapore, to bridge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In view of our unique vulnerabilities, I would like to make a few suggestions to SAF.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The DSI needs to be as much like Google and NSA, even as it retains its existing military culture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A key part of getting the culture right is being bold and innovative in the recruitment, growth and retention of cybersecurity talent.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, perhaps the salary structure of DIS may have to deviate considerably from the rest of the military.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope DIS can find ways of deploying our people to do very useful industry exchanges, attachments, or even sabbaticals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The obvious places for our people to spend time with are, of course, IT security companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we should not limit ourselves to that.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is an open secret to the security industry that there are certain countries with thriving pools of IT freelancers and experts capable of writing zero-day exploits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These exploits are then sold to cybersecurity firms, or even within the Dark Net.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Are we prepared to let our people go to those countries to immerse themselves in those complex environments?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because they will allow us to have a pulse of this rapidly evolving field.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, I hope that DIS should actively participate in defence exchanges with trusted countries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because national level threats and attacks can be of a different profile compared to isolated attacks on civilian and commercial IT systems.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even if the same tools are similar, the motivation, approach and the end goals are very different.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Three, I hope that DIS must ramp up and integrate with and defend the other services from cyberthreats quickly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, DIS could consider helping SAF architect our network architecture, so that certain basic capabilities can stay analogue, or even offline.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This can help us preserve basic capabilities, even in the face of an overwhelming attack, which requires time to resolve in cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope that DIS can be actively involved in securing our IT environment and processes as various SAF units conduct firmware updates of our software, weapons systems and communication systems.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, we should also be cautious of the silo effect.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: According to some industry experts, the key challenges that the US government face is the silo effect in achieving a stronger cybersecurity defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some commentators felt that NSA, given the nature of its mandate, was viewed as unwilling to share the full expertise and know-how with the Department of Homeland Security, which is in charge of cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singapore is too small a country to afford the luxury of turf wars, so I hope we bear that in mind as we have a fourth service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Four, we must safeguard of our capabilities very carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have the moral responsibility to ensure that the codes and tools do not get out, because of the potential unintended effect.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Doing so will also help our CSA sharpen their skills on how to keep our CII safe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: DIS should also help with defending non-military CII, because not all adversaries draw a line between military and civilian targets.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The creation of our fourth service DIS opens many new possibilities for SAF.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: SAF is now in a better position to supplement our existing capabilities with that of the private sector and to keep our military and non-military CII safe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: On that note, I would like to congratulate SAF for the creation of DIS and I wish success to the founding generation of DIS officers and staff.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of both Bills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore has never sought to be a military aggressor, we have never shied away from the need to build a technologically advanced, modern and competent SAF.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, today, I am proud to say, that SAF is a well-regarded fighting force, with possibly the best air and naval forces in the region.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore has excelled in our preparedness and readiness in conventional jungle and urban warfare, the strategies and tactics of war have changed considerably in recent years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The set-up of DIS is very timely in providing the much-needed safeguard to SAF's network assets as SAF transit, in earnest – to a firm, fighting 4G force.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In today's networked world, countries face a multitude of security threats on different fronts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the potential of open armed conflicts remains high, the actual possibility of countries openly engaging in hostile confrontations and conventional warfare, as what is happening in the Russo-Ukraine conflict, thankfully, remains low.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A more commonplace security threat in the 21st century is the invisible cyber warfare waged by state and non-state actors against countries, using cyber weapons that mask the identity of the aggressor.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such cyber attacks often go unnoticed by the man on the street as these attacks happen in cyberspace with low signatures in the physical realm, leaving no visible damages to real world infrastructures and assets until they actually happened.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Minister had said, "the battleground has changed".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is precisely because of the invisible and masked nature of such attacks that makes them so dangerous.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We tend to underestimate the devastating real life damages that such attacks could cause, and could possibly be underprepared for widespread cyber terrorism, or "hacktivist", attacks that assail multiple soft cyber targets simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike a physical infrastructure where we can adopt a more sectoral approach in defence, it is a little bit more challenging to do so in the case of cyber defence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, a network attack on the SAF can potentially cripple multiple systems at the same time and could possibly be difficult to isolate and contain.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the unlikely or unfortunate event of a cyber attack on SAF's system – which we hope would never happen – who would be ultimately responsible for the defence of the system?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would it be SAF's Defence Cyber Organisation (DCO)?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Cyber Defence Group (CDG) under SAF Command, Control, Communications, Computer and Intelligence (C4I)?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or would the defence be coordinated by SAF's Digital Ops-Tech Centre (DOTC), which has the mandate to partner with the Defence Tech Community (DTC) and whole-of-Government digital agencies to secure SAF's system?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And if the plan is for all the SAF units and platforms mentioned above to be coordinated under DIS, how would DIS liaise with CSA who is responsible for coordinating a whole-of-Government defence?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that Minister could provide some clarity on this later.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The catchment areas in Singapore, generally, comprise a majority of our reservoirs and natural landscape.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These areas contain a diverse range of flora and fauna, many of which are possibly still awaiting discovery.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, nine plants, fungi and algae were discovered, or re-discovered, in 2021, with more than half of these discovered in Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: NParks also reported in 2017 that 480 new species of flora and fauna were discovered, or rediscovered, in Singapore between 2012 and 2017.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, how does MINDEF intend to balance military needs which are critical and crucial, and I support, with public interest given that our catchment areas are family-friendly leisure locations frequented by leisure hikers and families who are seeking a respite from urban life?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What considerations would MINDEF have taken to ensure that the public's interest is catered for in these areas before embarking on such proposed manoeuvres?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am personally grateful to all of those who have served for their contributions to the nation and hope that the proposed amendments in the Bill will contribute to the further strengthening of our Armed Forces and other Services.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My clarifications notwithstanding, I end my speech in firm support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As established by my colleagues, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Dennis Tan, the Workers' Party has no fundamental objection to this newly established appointment and substantively support the Singapore Armed Forces and Other Matters Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most recently, at the Parliamentary debate on the Menon Constitutional Commission's report in 2016, the Workers' Party advocated returning to the elected presidency, to its original form to an appointed office without blocking powers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This will enable the President to focus on being a unifying figure for the nation, rather than having any confrontational role vis-à-vis the elected Government.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I must say that I was very impressed with every speech.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members did their research, have extensive knowledge way above the average citizen and they gave details of digital attacks elsewhere and how other militaries or agencies are addressing these threats and the difficulties faced.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think, perhaps, the first order of the day is to recruit some of them into the Digital and Intelligence Service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, do not be surprised if you get your SAF100.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The issue is how SAF does this and, in relation to DIS, their questions can be summed up in four areas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, why a formal service, a fourth, to add to the Army, Navy and Air Force?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, how will DIS meet manpower challenges, given our constraints and demands for IT-related skills?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, how will DIS and SAF work with partner organisations, such as the Home Team and CSA, to optimise our digital defences?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fourth, how will DIS guard against excesses and abuse of its powers and capabilities?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They are four important areas, so, let me address each in turn.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Don Wee asked about our considerations in deciding for a formal fourth service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This, indeed, was a critical issue that MINDEF and SAF leaders looked at extensively for some time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The manpower issue for DIS is, indeed, a serious challenge and I think almost all Members alluded to it – Mr Alex Yam, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Don Wee, Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They have highlighted this and given us good suggestions for recruitment and we will study their proposals seriously.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It provides their new entrants and existing staff career paths and progressions on par with the Army, Navy and Air Force, including for those with the aptitude to be Chief of Service, and even to be the Chief of Defence Force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Once formed, it puts the onus on the DIS leaders to fight for their fair or unfair share of talent that they need.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I completely agree with Members of this House that, indeed, there is a global demand for these types of skills, but this is healthy competition between the services first, and then, for the SAF to compete with the rest of the organisations that need that kind of talent.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For soldiers and personnel who join DIS, there will be a dedicated digital vocation which will develop experts in competencies, such as software engineering, app development, data science, AI, cloud architecting, among others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Talents in these fields will be eligible for top-tier SAF scholarships.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Compensation, as Members have supported, will be benchmarked against industry norms and regularly reviewed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The formation of DIS will boost their recruitment drives.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Already, we have our first SAF scholar who applied and was selected to join DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I met her last week during the presentation ceremony.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I joked with her that we have awarded her the scholarship on the assumption – because DIS has not been formed yet, because we have not passed the Bill – that Parliament approves the Bill and that the President assents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I told her, well, if Parliament or the President does not do what we hope they do, we will have to deploy her elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: She is doing law at Oxford and I think, perhaps, if Mr Vikram Nair will wait for a couple of years, she may be able to give him the answers to the questions that he asked about law and international relations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Just like other services, and perhaps with even more challenges, DIS must ensure that it provides an attractive proposition for jobseekers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It must provide job security, a good working environment and advancement opportunities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as Members here have pointed out, because it serves a higher calling, it must also bring in people with the right values and commitment and the mission mindset.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Sharael Taha reminded us, we need to be very security conscious.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They are guardians of our secrets and I agree with them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This mission mindset was the second key reason for our decision to form a fourth service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In its current configuration, the Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) community is a supporting force that supports the overall mission of the SAF and that of the Army, Navy and Air Force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As cyber warriors there, they are the frontline troops.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This mindset shift is crucial for the SAF as it builds the DIS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think this was the broader theme which Member Shawn Huang alluded to.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As a trained pilot, he knew to ask important strategic and tactical questions about missions for DIS and the key response for effective outcomes, whether for DIS personnel, soldiers, sailors or airmen, is the mission mindset.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I think the quick answer to Mr Vikram Nair's question – whether it could be a civilian chief – I would say no.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You need a military man in a uniform to have a military mindset.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, Mr Don Wee and Mr Dennis Tan asked about misinformation warfare and whether foreigners could be part of this force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singaporeans must, just like air, land and sea, be the core elements of this fourth service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Obviously, there will be services that they can outsource to third-party contractors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I agree with them – we have to be very careful even when we do that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There were other questions related to NSmen, and also whether soldiers in DIS would be trained and deployed differently, compared to the Army, Navy and Air Force.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about women – whether they could join as volunteers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I would like more women to join this if they are up to it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: My broad answer is that certain modules will remain common.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Without the right military values and mission mindset, there is a limit in using any individual soldier, no matter how talented he or she is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if someone serving National Service or a regular, has the aptitude and right attitude, I agree that such an individual can do more in DIS, even if his attributes are not best suited for physical combat.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I agree with Members that no single Ministry can do it alone.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Broadly, DIS will be external facing against potential aggressors, while the Home Team and CSA deal with threats internally.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as Members have pointed out, the cyber arena is much more porous than the physical domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Darryl David, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Henry Kwek, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Shawn Huang, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Gerald Giam asked how the DIS will organise itself and also complement and work with other relevant Government agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our agencies know that they cannot work in silos, lest the cyber attackers exploit gaps or poor coordination.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Inter-agency sharing of information, coordination and cooperation already exists.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our counter-terrorism efforts have taught us valuable lessons about whole-of-Government (WOG) responses and I cite this because it is a very good parallel example of interagency work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, similar to cyber threats, MINDEF and SAF are external facing for terrorism, working with foreign agencies to detect terrorists, either individually or their networks that mean to do us harm.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF set up the Counter Terrorism Information Facility (CTIF) to facilitate this work and share that information with external partners and local agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For cybersecurity, it will do the same, together with CSA.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Such coordination already exists today, so we are not starting on a blank sheet.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I can foresee exercises to test and improve multi-agency responses to common cyber threats, just as we do against terrorism.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if you remember, we have had multi-agencies exercises – when it comes to terrorism, I think there are as many as 10 or 11 agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have done exercises in ferry terminals, in Changi Airport, in the southern waters.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Digital Ops-Tech Centre (DOTC) will raise a core of practitioners who will apply their cross-cutting digital skills, such as in software development and Artificial Intelligence, towards operational outcomes for SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The digital range will provide a rich simulation environment for digital training and will host bilateral and multilateral exercises to bring together militaries, industry and academia to share best practices and insights.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Together, the DOTC and the digital range will form a strong foundation, from which the DIS will hone our digital defence capabilities and contribute to our digital defence, alongside the Home Team and CSA.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I visited such a cyber range, and this was in Estonia and the NATO Centre of Excellence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You build systems but there are water systems, power systems, support systems, hospital systems, so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They work with private practitioners and they are taught how to defend and, obviously, to act against penetration attacks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But these are the cyber troops that are raised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The mission and mandate, as scoped for the DIS to be primarily external-facing, reduce the risk of abuse and overstepping the SAF's authority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, Mr Louis Ng's characterisation of the DIS as a wide-ranging one is not quite accurate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In daily practice, the rules of engagement will also apply, just as it does to the SAF troops in civilian settings when they are guarding Changi Airport, Jurong Island or when they are deployed to deal with terrorist attacks or riots.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The rules of engagements are spelt out ex-ante to reduce the risk of abuse.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I was piqued by Members' grand vision for the DIS because it is not yet formed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some said that we should commercialise our successes and that we should share our secrets and capabilities with other agencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if abetment will be an offence that may be compounded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That will depend on the actual offence being abetted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For offences, such as those under the Penal Code, like abetting the assault of a superior officer, which I mentioned in my first speech, the maximum penalty has increased to seven years imprisonment to align with the Penal Code, and is not compoundable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For example, currently, if a soldier abets another into defaulting on IPPT, say by encouraging him to default or wilfully misleading him with inaccurate information on his IPPT requirements, both would have been charged.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: With the proposed amendments, both would have committed an offence which may be compounded.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was a question asked whether compared to summary trials, if compoundable offences, will be on your personal records.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The current system is that for all STs, it is on your records.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is very interesting with people discharged, we see all the offences, maybe some were even committed 20, 30 years ago for minor infractions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think it is balance between what we need to maintain military discipline and what the organisation really needs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And over time, I think we have found a new balance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, Mr Dennis Tan and I think Mr Louis Ng asked which specific offences will be put in the personal record and which ones will not.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will say, broadly, our most common offences are IPPT infractions and smoking in non-designated areas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If Members push very hard, I will try and keep that on the personal record.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if you repeatedly miss an IPPT, or purposefully go against the superior's order not to smoke in the area, that is a very different kind of situation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether it was a discharge and acquittal.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It again depends on whether there is a charge against the offence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Once the composition sum is paid, no further proceedings are to be taken against the accused for that alleged offence, as reflected in the proposed section 79A(4) of the SAF Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the Public Prosecutor will provide directions for how authorised composition officers should exercise their composition powers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For increased fine limits, Mr Louis Ng is broadly accurate that the fine limits under section 118 have increased significantly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, sections 68, 69, 70, 70A, 70B and 72 will be amended for higher fine limits but to different degrees.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even with the increase in fine limits, it remains for the military courts and disciplinary officers to assess the specific circumstances of the case and to decide on the appropriate fine to impose.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are just raising the limit, but the powers are still theirs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and SAF have established guidelines on fine amounts, based on offence severity and the rank of the offender, and will adjust these guidelines as he has asked for, when the amendments of the Act take effect.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Ng asked whether the military court would consider the impact of the preceding civil proceedings and any sentences served by the accused for related civil offences, when imposing a sentence for the military offences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before preferring charges against the serviceman in the military court, MINDEF will assess all available information and findings which may be relevant, including, but not limited to, the findings and sentences by the civil courts in related civil proceedings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Darryl David and Mr Dennis Tan asked about the environmental impact and public security of military manoeuvres in catchment areas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I feel a little embarrassed about this amendment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are just regularising what all of us as NSmen have gone through.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of us, I think, have been into Mandai Reservoir, Kranji Reservoir; some got lost, maybe.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Thankfully, I did not; or maybe, I helped somebody get lost; never mind.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we had an agreement with PUB, I think, as far back as in the 1990s to train there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we are regularising it to say that now, we can only exercise if PUB says we can.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: People asked about the environmental impact from such training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have been doing it for 40-over years under very strict guidelines that protect our catchment area, water especially.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Biodiversity – there have been environmental impact assessments done from time to time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I want to sound a word of caution: we do not have much terrain to train in.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if we say, "Oh, your training can affect", as Mr Darryl David said, "one of nine particular fauna or flora", we may have very limited land to train in.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, please bear that in mind when you are pushing to protect biodiversity – as all of us want to, but there is a balance to be struck.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The three services of the SAF were established in 1972 with the enactment of the SAF Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, 50 years on, the amendments today bring into existence a fourth service.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It provides the SAF with the right structure and emphasis to continue building a full suite of capabilities that can protect Singapore's sovereignty and independence, whether on land, sea, in the air and in the digital domain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Once again, let me thank the Members who have spoken on the Bill and for their support.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister said that DIS will compete with other organisations for tech talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am concerned that this would further exacerbate the talent crunch in the private sector, especially for SMEs who cannot provide the same salary scales of the Government or MNCs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Besides scholarships, what is MINDEF's plan for increasing the pipeline for tech talent in Singapore to feed into DIS and other organisations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: For example, will MINDEF be working with MOE to help our IHLs increase their Singaporean intake for IT-related majors?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They will have a budget to work with.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We say that the DIS is important and we say manpower is important.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is the task of the commanders to make it attractive to grow the pie to bring people in.      .
